slides.title: Network implementation
slides.sub: Domain 2: routing, switching, wireless, and physical installs
slides.say: Welcome to domain two of the Network Plus N10-009 exam: network implementation. It is worth twenty percent of the exam. We will cover routing, switching features, wireless, and the physical factors of an installation.

slides.title: 2.1 Routing basics
head: Concept
Key facts
rows: Manual, no overhead, does not adapt
Routers share routes and adapt to failures
Longest prefix match first, then AD, then metric
Translate private addresses; PAT uses ports
slides.say: Start with routing. A static route is entered by hand, adds no overhead, and does not adapt to failures. Dynamic routing lets routers share routes and adapt. The default route, zero dot zero dot zero dot zero slash zero, is the route of last resort. When several routes match, the router picks the longest prefix match first, then the lowest administrative distance, then the best metric. Remember the distances: connected zero, static one, O S P F one-ten, and R I P one-twenty. N A T translates private addresses, and P A T lets many hosts share one public address by using port numbers.

slides.title: 2.1 Dynamic routing protocols
head: Protocol
Type
Remember
slides.callout: FHRP: routers share a virtual IP so the default gateway survives a failure. HSRP and GLBP are Cisco; VRRP is open.
slides.say: The routing protocols. R I P is a distance vector protocol that counts hops, with a maximum of fifteen. O S P F is a link-state protocol, an open standard that uses cost and areas. E I G R P is Cisco's advanced distance vector protocol, with an administrative distance of ninety. And B G P is a path vector protocol that runs between autonomous systems, which is how the internet is stitched together. Also know first hop redundancy: routers share a virtual I P address so the default gateway survives a failure. H S R P and G L B P are Cisco, and V R R P is an open standard.

slides.title: 2.2 VLANs and trunks
items: VLANs split one switch into separate broadcast domains
Access port: carries one VLAN, untagged
Trunk port: carries many VLANs with 802.1Q tags
Native VLAN: the untagged VLAN on a trunk; both ends must match
Inter-VLAN traffic needs a router or Layer 3 switch
Voice VLAN separates phone traffic
slides.say: Now switching. V LANs split a switch into separate broadcast domains. An access port carries one V LAN, untagged. A trunk port carries many V LANs using eight oh two dot one Q tags. The native V LAN is the untagged V LAN on a trunk, and both ends must match. Traffic between V LANs needs a router or a layer three switch. A voice V LAN keeps phone traffic separate from data.

slides.title: 2.2 Spanning tree and link aggregation
head: Feature
What to know
rows: Blocks redundant links to prevent loops
Lowest bridge ID; all paths lead to it
Converges much faster than classic STP
Bundle links into one; LACP is the open standard
Copies traffic to an analyzer port
slides.say: Spanning tree blocks redundant links to prevent loops. The switch with the lowest bridge I D becomes the root bridge. Ports take roles: root ports face the root, designated ports forward, and alternate ports block. Rapid S T P converges much faster than the classic version. Link aggregation bundles several links into one logical link for bandwidth and redundancy, and L A C P is the open standard. Spanning tree treats the bundle as one link, so it does not block it. Port mirroring copies traffic to an analyzer port.

slides.title: 2.2 Switch features
head: Feature
Purpose
rows: Shut a port that receives BPDUs
MTU up to about 9000 for storage
slides.say: Know the common switch features. Port security limits the mac addresses on a port. D H C P snooping blocks rogue D H C P servers. B P D U guard shuts down a port that receives spanning tree messages, such as when someone plugs in a switch. Power over Ethernet comes in levels: eight oh two dot three A F delivers about fifteen watts, A T about thirty, and B T up to ninety. Jumbo frames raise the M T U to about nine thousand bytes, and are used for storage traffic. And Q o S prioritizes voice and video.

slides.title: 2.3 Wi-Fi standards and bands
head: Standard
Name
Bands
slides.callout: 2.4 GHz: longest range, most interference, non-overlapping channels 1, 6, and 11.
slides.say: Wireless. Eight oh two dot eleven N is Wi-Fi four, on two point four and five gigahertz. A C is Wi-Fi five, on five gigahertz. A X is Wi-Fi six, and six E adds the six gigahertz band. B E is Wi-Fi seven. Two point four gigahertz has the longest range but the most interference, and its non-overlapping channels are one, six, and eleven. Five gigahertz has more channels and less interference but shorter range.

slides.title: 2.3 Wireless security and design
items: WPA2 uses AES; WPA3 uses SAE and resists offline guessing
Enterprise mode uses 802.1X with a RADIUS server
SSID is the name; BSSID is one radio; ESSID spans many access points
Band steering pushes capable clients to 5 GHz
Site survey and heat map plan coverage
Lightweight APs are managed by a wireless controller
slides.say: For wireless security, W P A two uses A E S, and W P A three uses S A E, which resists offline password guessing. Enterprise mode uses eight oh two dot one X with a radius server. The S S I D is the network name, the B S S I D identifies one radio, and the E S S I D is one network across many access points. Band steering moves capable clients to five gigahertz. Site surveys and heat maps plan coverage. And lightweight access points are managed by a wireless controller.

slides.title: 2.3 Antennas and modes
items: Omnidirectional: coverage in all directions
Directional: focused signal for point-to-point links
Infrastructure mode: clients connect through an access point
Ad hoc: devices connect directly
Mesh: access points relay traffic wirelessly
Channel width: wider is faster but picks up more interference
slides.say: Antennas and modes. Omnidirectional antennas cover all directions. Directional antennas focus the signal for long point-to-point links. In infrastructure mode, clients connect through an access point. In ad hoc mode, devices connect directly. In a mesh, access points relay traffic wirelessly. And remember that wider channels are faster but pick up more interference.

slides.title: 2.4 Physical installation
items: Rack units: 1U is 1.75 inches
Patch panels, and 110 or 66 punchdown blocks
MDF is the main closet; IDF is a closet on a floor
Plenum-rated cable for air-handling spaces
Hot aisle and cold aisle airflow; keep fiber bends gentle
UPS, PDU, and redundant power; label every cable
slides.say: Finally, physical installation. A rack unit, one U, is one point seven five inches. Cables terminate on patch panels and on one-ten or sixty-six punchdown blocks. The M D F is the main distribution closet, and an I D F is a closet on a floor. Use plenum-rated cable in air-handling spaces. Arrange racks in hot aisles and cold aisles for cooling. Provide U P S and P D U power, with redundancy, and label every cable. A fiber distribution panel organizes fiber connections.

slides.title: Domain 2 recap
items: Route choice: longest prefix, then AD, then metric
Know the protocols and their types
Access vs trunk, native VLAN, STP roles
Know PoE levels and Wi-Fi standards
Plan power, cooling, and labeling
slides.say: To recap domain two: remember the route selection order, know each protocol and its type, understand access and trunk ports and the native V LAN, and know the spanning tree roles. Know the P o E levels and the Wi-Fi standards, and plan power, cooling, and labeling. Good luck.
